The English founded colonies in North America - Jamestown, Virginia (1607), Plymouth (Pilgrims, 1620) and Massachusetts Bay - and in the Caribbean (Barbados, Jamaica), and the English East India Company traded in India.

The French established New France (Quebec, 1608, by Samuel de Champlain), Louisiana and Caribbean colonies (Saint-Domingue). Plantation economies of sugar, tobacco and later cotton relied on enslaved Africans; the Atlantic slave trade carried about 12 million Africans to the Americas between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, in the 'triangular trade' between Europe, Africa and the Americas. Mercantilist rivalries led to wars (Anglo-Dutch Wars) and, in the eighteenth century, Anglo-French conflicts in India and North America.
section-84: Causes: the financial crisis of the French monarchy (due to wars, including support for the American Revolution, and court extravagance); an unjust social system of three estates - clergy (First Estate), nobility (Second Estate) and everyone else (Third Estate), who paid most taxes; Enlightenment ideas (Voltaire, Montesquieu's separation of powers, Rousseau's 'Social Contract' and general will); bad harvests and high bread prices (1788-1789); and the example of the American Revolution. Louis XVI called the Estates-General in May 1789.

Course: the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly (Tennis Court Oath, 20 June 1789); the storming of the Bastille (14 July 1789); the abolition of feudal privileges (4 August); the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (26 August); the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (1790); and the constitutional monarchy (1791). War with Austria and Prussia (1792) and popular radicalisation (the sans-culottes) led to the overthrow of the monarchy and the First Republic (September 1792); Louis XVI was executed (January 1793). The Jacobins under Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety ran the Reign of Terror (1793-1794), executing thousands by the guillotine, until Robespierre fell (Thermidor, July 1794). The Directory (1795-1799) was weak and corrupt; Napoleon Bonaparte's coup (18 Brumaire, November 1799) established the Consulate, and he became Emperor in 1804. The Revolution spread ideals of liberty, equality, fraternity, popular sovereignty and nationalism.
section-86: Background: the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople (1453) and control of the eastern Mediterranean raised the cost of Asian spices and silk; Venetian and Genoese merchants dominated existing routes; Catalan, Venetian and Genoese commercial colonies developed techniques of colonial plantation, banking and navigation. A bullion shortage encouraged the search for African gold. The Reconquista (completed in 1492 with the conquest of Granada) gave Spain and Portugal crusading zeal and experience.

Portuguese expansion: Ceuta (1415), Prince Henry's patronage of exploration, caravels and navigational instruments, the African coast (gold and slaves at Elmina), Dias's rounding of the Cape (1488), da Gama's arrival at Calicut (1498), and the Estado da India (Goa, Malacca, Hormuz). Spanish expansion: Columbus (1492), the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494), Magellan's circumnavigation (1519-1522, completed by Elcano), the conquest of the Aztecs (Cortés, 1521) and Incas (Pizarro, 1532), silver mines (Potosí), the encomienda and the destruction of indigenous populations by disease and exploitation.

Consequences: the shift of Europe's economic centre from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic; the 'Columbian Exchange' of plants, animals and diseases; the Price Revolution due to American silver; the beginning of the Atlantic slave trade; the rise of commercial capitalism; and European colonial domination of large parts of the world. Historians emphasise both European agency and the violence suffered by indigenous peoples.
section-87: Renaissance: began in Italy in the fourteenth century with Petrarch and spread across Europe by the sixteenth century. Features: humanism and the revival of classical learning; individualism and secular interests; patronage by wealthy families (the Medici) and popes; achievements in art (perspective, realism - Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael), architecture (Brunelleschi's dome in Florence), literature (Machiavelli, Erasmus, More, Shakespeare) and science (Copernicus, Vesalius). The printing press (Gutenberg, c. 1450) spread ideas and contributed to the Reformation.

Reformations: the Lutheran Reformation (1517) challenged indulgences, papal authority and church doctrine with justification by faith, the authority of the Bible and the priesthood of all believers; it spread with support from German princes, ending with the Peace of Augsburg (1555). Calvinism (Geneva) spread to France (Huguenots), the Netherlands, Scotland (John Knox) and England (Puritans). The English Reformation (1534) under Henry VIII was political at first; the Elizabethan Settlement (1559) created a moderate Anglican church.

Catholic Reformation: the Council of Trent (1545-1563) reaffirmed doctrine and reformed abuses; the Jesuits (1540) promoted education and missions; the Inquisition and Index suppressed heresy. Consequences: the end of religious unity in western Europe, religious wars, strengthening of state power over churches, growth of literacy and vernacular languages, and, according to Max Weber ('The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism', 1905), a link between Protestant values and the rise of capitalism (a debated thesis).
section-88: Economic and social instability: the Price Revolution (inflation due to American silver, population growth and debasement) hurt wage earners and landlords with fixed incomes; peasant revolts and state bankruptcies occurred. Wars of religion: in France (1562-1598), between Catholics and Huguenots (St Bartholomew's Day Massacre, 1572; Edict of Nantes, 1598); in the Netherlands (Dutch Revolt, 1568-1648), against Spanish rule and Catholic repression, leading to the Dutch Republic; and in Germany (Schmalkaldic War; Peace of Augsburg).

International rivalry: Spain under Philip II was the leading Catholic power, but the defeat of the Armada (1588) by England under Elizabeth I weakened it. The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) began as a religious conflict in Bohemia and became a European power struggle involving Denmark, Sweden and France; it devastated Germany. The Peace of Westphalia (1648) established the principle of state sovereignty and religious coexistence. France under Richelieu and Mazarin rose to dominance.

English Civil War (1642-1651): caused by conflicts over royal power, taxation and religion between the Stuart kings and Parliament; it led to the execution of Charles I (1649), the Commonwealth and Cromwell's Protectorate, the Restoration (1660) and finally the Glorious Revolution (1688) and the Bill of Rights (1689), establishing constitutional monarchy. These conflicts transformed political thought (Hobbes, Locke) and laid foundations of modern European states.
section-89: Absolutism: rulers such as Louis XIV of France (Versailles, intendants, Colbert's mercantilism, revocation of the Edict of Nantes, expensive wars) claimed unlimited divine-right authority, supported by theorists like Bodin, Hobbes and Bossuet. In Central and Eastern Europe, Habsburg Austria, Hohenzollern Prussia and Romanov Russia built strong states. Peter the Great westernised Russia, founded St Petersburg and created a modern army; Catherine the Great expanded Russia and strengthened serfdom.

Colonial expansion: the Dutch, English and French built empires in Asia, the Americas and Africa; plantation economies relied on the Atlantic slave trade; mercantilism viewed colonies as sources of raw materials and markets; and rivalries led to wars. The Enlightenment (Locke, Montesquieu, Voltaire, Rousseau, Diderot's Encyclopédie) criticised absolutism, privilege and religious intolerance, promoting reason, natural rights and the social contract.

French Revolution: financial crisis, social inequality of the three estates, Enlightenment ideas and food shortages led to the Estates-General (1789), the National Assembly, the fall of the Bastille, the abolition of feudalism and the Declaration of the Rights of Man. Radicalisation produced the Republic (1792), the execution of the king (1793) and the Reign of Terror under Robespierre (1793-1794). The Thermidorian reaction and the Directory (1795-1799) followed, ending with Napoleon's Consulate (1799). The Revolution introduced ideas of popular sovereignty, nationalism, equality before law and secular government that shaped the modern world.
section-92: In the American tradition, archaeology is considered one of the four fields of anthropology (with cultural, biological and linguistic anthropology). Lewis Binford's article 'Archaeology as Anthropology' (1962) launched the 'New Archaeology' or processual archaeology, which argued that archaeology should explain human behaviour and cultural processes - such as adaptation to environment, economic systems and social organisation - not merely describe artefacts.

Archaeologists use ethnoarchaeology (studying living communities to understand how material remains are formed) and ethnographic analogy to interpret the past. For example, studying modern potters in India helps interpret ancient pottery production. This approach treats culture as a system, with technology, economy, social structure and ideology interrelated.
section-93: In Europe and India, archaeology has often been closely linked with history. It provides evidence for periods without writing (prehistory) and for groups whose lives were not recorded in written texts - peasants, artisans, women, slaves. It can confirm, correct or supplement texts: for example, excavations at Hastinapura and Ayodhya were used to examine traditions in the epics, while excavations of Mughal and colonial sites add to knowledge of later periods.

Historical archaeology studies periods with written records, combining texts and material evidence; examples include excavations of Harappan, Mauryan (Pataliputra), Kushana and medieval sites. Post-processual archaeologists (Ian Hodder) emphasise that material culture has meaning and must be interpreted historically, like a text, considering human agency and context.
section-94: Archaeology uses scientific methods: systematic survey and excavation, precise recording (plans, sections, photographs, GPS and GIS), and laboratory analysis. Scientific techniques include radiocarbon dating, thermoluminescence, dendrochronology, DNA analysis of human and animal remains, stable isotope analysis (to find out about diet and migration), archaeobotany (study of plant remains, including pollen and phytoliths), archaeozoology (animal bones), geoarchaeology (soils and sediments), metallurgy and remote sensing (aerial photography, satellite images, LiDAR, ground-penetrating radar).

Processual archaeologists in the 1960s argued that archaeology should use scientific methods of hypothesis testing to explain cultural change. Today archaeology is interdisciplinary, combining humanities and natural sciences.
section-95: The scope of archaeology is very wide in time - from the earliest stone tools (over three million years ago) to the recent past (industrial archaeology, the archaeology of the World Wars and even modern rubbish, 'garbology') - and in subject. Specialised fields include prehistoric archaeology, historical archaeology, classical archaeology, underwater or maritime archaeology (for example, at Dwarka in Gujarat), environmental archaeology, bioarchaeology, ethnoarchaeology, experimental archaeology, landscape archaeology and public archaeology.

Archaeology studies settlements and architecture, technology and crafts, subsistence and diet, trade and exchange networks, social organisation and inequality, religion and ritual, burial practices, health and disease, migration, environment and climate. It also contributes to heritage management, tourism and national identity.
section-96: Ethical issues include: (1) excavation is destructive, so archaeologists must record everything carefully and publish their results; (2) looting and the illegal antiquities trade destroy context - UNESCO's 1970 Convention and India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act (1972) try to prevent this; (3) human remains should be treated with respect and in consultation with descendant communities, as in the USA's Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA, 1990); (4) repatriation of artefacts taken during colonial times (the Elgin Marbles, Benin Bronzes, the Koh-i-Noor debate).

Other issues include the rights of local and indigenous communities over their heritage, the political misuse of archaeology for nationalist or communal purposes (for example, debates over religious sites), conservation of sites threatened by development, tourism and war, and honest interpretation without exaggeration. Professional bodies such as the World Archaeological Congress have codes of ethics.
section-97: The speculative or antiquarian phase (before the mid-nineteenth century) involved collecting antiquities and curiosities, often by wealthy individuals, without systematic methods. Renaissance collectors gathered classical sculptures; William Camden (England) and others described ancient monuments. Interpretations were often based on the Bible (Archbishop Ussher dated creation to 4004 BCE) or imagination; for example, Stonehenge was attributed to the Druids or Romans.

Early excavations, such as those at Pompeii and Herculaneum (from 1738 and 1748) and Thomas Jefferson's careful excavation of a burial mound in Virginia (1784), began to change this. Napoleon's expedition to Egypt (1798) led to the discovery of the Rosetta Stone, which Champollion used to decipher hieroglyphs (1822). In India, the Asiatic Society (1784) began antiquarian studies.
section-98: Key developments: the Danish scholar C. J. Thomsen's Three Age System (Stone, Bronze, Iron, 1836); the acceptance of the antiquity of humankind (Boucher de Perthes and the work of Pengelly at Brixham Cave, 1859) and Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species' (1859); General Pitt-Rivers' systematic excavations and recording (1880s); Flinders Petrie's seriation (sequence dating) of Egyptian pottery; Heinrich Schliemann's excavation of Troy (1870s); V. Gordon Childe's culture-historical approach and concepts of the Neolithic and Urban Revolutions; Mortimer Wheeler's grid method of excavation (the 'Wheeler box') and stratigraphic control; and radiocarbon dating (Willard Libby, 1949).

Later theoretical schools include processual archaeology (Lewis Binford, 1960s), which used scientific methods and systems theory, and post-processual archaeology (Ian Hodder, 1980s), which emphasised meaning, symbolism, agency and multiple interpretations. Today archaeology also includes feminist, Marxist and indigenous perspectives and new technologies (GIS, LiDAR, DNA). In India, the ASI, H. D. Sankalia, B. B. Lal and others developed modern archaeology.
section-99: Artefacts are portable objects made or modified by humans - tools, pottery, coins, ornaments, weapons. Features are non-portable human-made traces - hearths, pits, post-holes, walls, floors, drains. Structures are buildings and monuments. Ecofacts are natural remains that show human activity or environment - seeds, pollen, animal bones, shells, charcoal. Human remains (skeletons, mummies) give information on health, diet, age, sex, migration (through isotopes) and ancestry (through DNA).

Sites are places with concentrations of evidence; landscapes include whole areas shaped by human activity (fields, roads, terraces). Inscriptions and coins are also archaeological evidence. The meaning of evidence depends on its context - where it was found and in association with what.
section-100: Michael Schiffer ('Formation Processes of the Archaeological Record', 1987) distinguished between cultural (C-transforms) and natural (N-transforms) formation processes. Cultural formation processes include: manufacture and use of objects; deliberate burial (graves, hoards, foundation deposits); discard of rubbish in middens and pits; loss; abandonment of sites (orderly or sudden, as at Pompeii); reuse and recycling of materials (bricks from old buildings reused in new ones, as at Harappa, where railway builders used bricks as ballast in the 1850s); and later disturbance such as ploughing, construction, looting and earlier excavation.

Understanding these processes is essential because the archaeological record is not a direct picture of past life. For example, a house floor may contain only items left at abandonment, not all items used. Archaeologists must reconstruct how deposits formed before interpreting them.
section-101: Natural formation processes include decay and decomposition of organic materials (wood, leather, textiles, food), which survive only in special conditions - extreme dryness (Egypt), waterlogging (bogs, lake dwellings), freezing (the 'Iceman' Ötzi in the Alps) or charring. Other natural processes are erosion and deposition by rivers, wind and sea; flooding, which buried and preserved some sites; volcanic eruptions (Pompeii, 79 CE); earthquakes; and the action of animals (burrowing rodents, earthworms) and plant roots (bioturbation), which can move objects between layers.

Soil chemistry also matters: acidic soils destroy bone, while alkaline soils preserve it. Archaeologists must understand these processes to interpret what survives and to avoid misreading the position of finds.
section-102: Context includes the matrix (the sediment surrounding a find), the provenience (the exact three-dimensional location of a find, recorded with coordinates and depth) and the association (other finds and features found with it). Primary context is undisturbed since deposition; secondary context has been disturbed by later human or natural processes.

Context is what gives an artefact its historical meaning. For example, a coin found in a sealed floor layer can date that floor; a pot found in a grave tells us about burial practice; but the same objects bought from an antique dealer tell us very little. This is why looting is so damaging and why careful recording during excavation is essential. Context also allows archaeologists to build chronology through stratigraphy.
section-103: Archaeological survey locates, maps and records sites without excavating them, or as a preliminary to excavation. Methods include: (1) studying maps, historical documents, place names and local traditions; (2) field walking - systematically walking over fields to collect surface finds such as potsherds and tools; (3) aerial photography, which can reveal buried features as crop marks or soil marks; (4) satellite imagery and LiDAR (laser scanning that can 'see' through vegetation, used at Angkor and Maya sites); and (5) geophysical survey - magnetometry, electrical resistivity and ground-penetrating radar.

Surveys can be regional, studying settlement patterns across a landscape (for example, the surveys of the Ghaggar-Hakra valley that located many Harappan sites). They are less destructive and less expensive than excavation and help select sites for excavation.
section-104: Excavation is the controlled digging of a site to recover evidence and understand its sequence. Methods: vertical excavation (trenches or test pits to reveal the sequence of layers through time) and horizontal or open-area excavation (exposing a large area of one layer to study the plan of a settlement at one time). Mortimer Wheeler's grid or box method combined both, leaving baulks (walls of earth) between squares to show sections. Philip Barker and Edward Harris introduced open-area excavation and the Harris Matrix to record stratigraphy.

Every find, layer and feature must be recorded with drawings, photographs, descriptions and measurements, because excavation destroys the site. Finds are labelled, cleaned, conserved and analysed. Results must be published so that others can use the information. Excavation is expensive and time-consuming, so many archaeologists prefer survey and minimal excavation where possible.
section-105: Stratigraphy is based on the principle of superposition, borrowed from geology (Nicolas Steno, Charles Lyell): in undisturbed deposits, lower layers are older than upper layers. Each layer (stratum) represents a period of deposition. Archaeologists record layers in vertical sections and identify the sequence of deposits, features (such as pits cut into earlier layers) and interfaces.

Stratigraphy gives relative dates - it shows that one layer is older or younger than another, but not by how many years. Objects found in a layer are generally dated to the period of that layer, so a sequence of pottery types can be established. Disturbances such as pits, burrows and later building can complicate stratigraphy; the Harris Matrix (Edward Harris, 1973) is a diagram used to show stratigraphic relationships.
section-106: Typology classifies artefacts into types based on shared features of form, material, decoration and technique. Archaeologists assume that styles change over time in a gradual way, so artefacts can be arranged in a developmental sequence. Oscar Montelius (Sweden) developed typological sequences for Bronze Age objects in the late nineteenth century.

Seriation, developed by Flinders Petrie for Egyptian graves (sequence dating, 1899), arranges assemblages in order according to the frequency of different types: a new style appears, becomes popular and then declines (a 'battleship curve'). In India, pottery types such as Black-and-Red Ware, Painted Grey Ware and Northern Black Polished Ware help date sites. Typology gives relative dates and also helps identify cultural groups and trade.
section-107: Dendrochronology (tree-ring dating) was developed by the American astronomer A. E. Douglass in the early twentieth century. Trees in temperate regions add one growth ring each year; ring widths vary with climate (wide in good years, narrow in dry or cold years). By matching patterns of ring widths from living trees, old timbers and archaeological wood, scientists have built continuous master chronologies going back over 12,000 years in some regions (for example, oak and pine chronologies in Europe and bristlecone pine in California).

It can date wood very precisely - sometimes to the exact year the tree was felled. It is also used to calibrate radiocarbon dates and to study past climate (dendroclimatology). Limitations: it works only for certain species in regions with clear seasons, requires samples with enough rings, and dates the tree's growth rather than the use of the wood, which may have been reused.
section-108: Radiocarbon (C-14) dating was developed by Willard Libby in 1949 (Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 1960). All living organisms absorb carbon, including a small amount of radioactive carbon-14. After death, C-14 decays at a known rate - its half-life is about 5,730 years. By measuring the remaining C-14 in organic material (charcoal, bone, wood, seeds, shells), scientists estimate the time since death, up to about 50,000 years. Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AMS) allows dating of very small samples. Dates are calibrated using tree rings because the amount of atmospheric C-14 has varied.

Other radiometric methods include potassium-argon and argon-argon dating (for volcanic rocks, used for early hominin sites in East Africa, millions of years old), uranium-series dating (for cave deposits and corals), thermoluminescence (TL) for pottery and burnt flint, and optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) for sediments, which measure the time since last heating or exposure to light. Results are given as a date with a margin of error (for example, 3000 ± 50 BP, 'before present', meaning before 1950).
section-109: Relative dating places events or objects in sequence (earlier or later) without giving calendar dates. Methods include stratigraphy, typology and seriation, cross-dating (dating objects in one area by comparison with dated objects elsewhere - for example, Harappan seals found in dated Mesopotamian contexts), fluorine testing of bones (which exposed the Piltdown Man hoax in 1953), and linguistic dating (estimating the time languages diverged).

Absolute (chronometric) dating gives dates in years or date ranges. Methods include historical dating (calendars, inscriptions, coins, king lists), dendrochronology, radiocarbon and other radiometric methods, luminescence, and genetic dating (estimating the time of population splits from mutation rates in DNA). Climatic events recorded in ice cores, varves (annual lake sediments) and pollen sequences also help build chronologies. Archaeologists usually combine several methods for reliable chronology.
section-111: Definition and aims: archaeology is the study of the human past through material remains. Its aims are to reconstruct past lifeways (how people lived), establish chronology and culture history, explain cultural change (processual archaeology) and understand meanings and agency (post-processual archaeology). Archaeology as anthropology (Binford) studies human behaviour and culture systems; archaeology as history reconstructs past societies, especially those without written records; archaeology as science uses systematic methods and laboratory techniques.

Scope: archaeology covers all periods from the earliest humans to the recent past and all aspects of life - settlement, economy, technology, social organisation, religion, environment, health and trade. Specialised fields include prehistoric, historical, classical, underwater, environmental, ethno-, experimental and public archaeology.

Ethics: excavation destroys sites, so recording and publication are obligations. Archaeologists must oppose looting and illegal trade, respect human remains and descendant communities, consider repatriation, protect heritage from development and conflict, involve local communities and resist the political misuse of archaeology. Laws such as India's Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act (1958) and international conventions (UNESCO 1970, World Heritage 1972) provide legal frameworks.
section-112: History of the discipline: the speculative or antiquarian phase involved collecting antiquities and speculation (often based on the Bible); the nineteenth century brought the Three Age System (Thomsen), the antiquity of humankind and Darwin's theory, Pitt-Rivers' and Petrie's systematic methods; the twentieth century saw Childe's culture history, Wheeler's stratigraphic excavation, radiocarbon dating (Libby), processual archaeology (Binford) and post-processual archaeology (Hodder). In India, the Asiatic Society, Cunningham's ASI, Marshall's discovery of the Indus civilisation, Wheeler's reforms and postcolonial research shaped the field.

Evidence: artefacts, features, structures, ecofacts, human remains, sites and landscapes. Formation processes: cultural (manufacture, use, discard, burial, abandonment, reuse, later disturbance) and natural (decay, erosion, flooding, volcanic eruptions, bioturbation, soil chemistry) - both shape what survives and where. Preservation varies greatly; organic materials survive only in special conditions.

Context: the matrix, provenience and association of finds are essential for interpretation. Primary contexts are undisturbed; secondary contexts have been disturbed. Without context, as with looted objects, artefacts lose most of their historical value. Understanding formation processes and context allows archaeologists to make valid inferences about past human behaviour.
section-113: Survey: non-destructive methods to find and map sites - documentary research, field walking, aerial photography, satellite imagery, LiDAR and geophysical survey (magnetometry, resistivity, ground-penetrating radar). Regional surveys reveal settlement patterns. Excavation: vertical trenches for sequence, horizontal open-area excavation for plans, Wheeler's grid method; careful recording through plans, sections, photographs, context sheets and the Harris Matrix; and publication of results.

Relative dating: stratigraphy (superposition), typology and seriation (Montelius, Petrie), cross-dating, fluorine testing, linguistic dating (glottochronology) and climatic sequences (pollen zones, ice cores). Absolute dating: historical calendars and inscriptions; dendrochronology (exact years; calibration of radiocarbon); radiocarbon (half-life 5,730 years, up to about 50,000 years, AMS); potassium-argon and argon-argon (millions of years); uranium series; thermoluminescence and OSL; and genetic dating using DNA mutation rates.

Archaeologists combine methods to build reliable chronologies and cross-check results. For example, the dates of the Harappan civilisation are based on radiocarbon dates, stratigraphy and cross-dating with Mesopotamia. Accurate chronology allows comparison of sites across regions and the reconstruction of processes such as the spread of agriculture or urbanisation.
